title: iPad (11th generation) battery replacement
diagnosis: A battery that drains quickly is usually worn out after many charge cycles, so I'll plan a battery replacement. This is a hard repair on an iPad because the display is glued on and the cells are held with stretch-release strips.
safety_notes: Let the iPad battery run below 25% before starting.
Never puncture, bend or pry the battery cells with metal tools.
If a cell is swollen, hot or leaking, stop and take it to a professional.
Wear safety glasses when lifting the glass.

steps.title: Power off and warm the edges
steps.instruction: Hold the top button and power the iPad off, then unplug any cable. Warm the display edges with a heat mat or hairdryer for about two minutes.
steps.expected_visual_state: The iPad screen is black with no cable attached, lying face up with a heat source on the edges.
common_mistakes: Skipping the power-off step
Overheating one spot and damaging the LCD
Using a metal tool too early

steps.title: Separate the display
steps.instruction: Attach a suction handle and slide a plastic pick into the gap along the edge. Work around slowly, keeping the pick shallow, and lift the display open like a book.
steps.expected_visual_state: The display is lifted slightly and rests beside the shell, still connected by its flex cables.
common_mistakes: Inserting the pick too deep and cutting the display flex
Prying hard instead of re-heating
Pulling the display fully away

steps.title: Disconnect the battery first
steps.instruction: Remove the four screws from the display cable bracket and lift it off. Use a plastic spudger to pop the battery connector straight up.
steps.expected_visual_state: The bracket is set aside and the battery flex connector is lifted away from the logic board.
common_mistakes: Losing the tiny screws
Prying at the connector's side instead of lifting it straight up
Leaving the battery connected

steps.title: Disconnect the display
steps.instruction: Pop the display and digitizer connectors with the spudger. Lift the display away and put it aside safely.
steps.expected_visual_state: The display is fully removed, exposing both battery cells and the logic board.
common_mistakes: Pulling the flex cables instead of unclipping them
Putting the display down where it can get scratched

steps.title: Release the old cells
steps.instruction: Pull each stretch-release strip slowly and flat along the cell, as low and straight as you can. Lift the left and right cells out of the shell.
steps.expected_visual_state: The old battery cells are out of the shell and the empty battery bays are visible.
common_mistakes: Pulling the strips upward so they snap
Prying the cells with a metal tool
Bending the cells

steps.title: Fit the new battery
steps.instruction: Clean the bays, apply new adhesive strips and place the new cells. Press them down gently and connect the battery flex.
steps.expected_visual_state: The new cells sit flat in the shell with the battery connector clipped onto the logic board.
common_mistakes: Leaving old adhesive in the bays
Placing the cells misaligned
Not seating the battery connector fully

steps.title: Reconnect the display and close
steps.instruction: Reconnect the display and digitizer connectors and refit the bracket with its four screws. Lower the display, press the edges to seal, and let it set.
steps.expected_visual_state: The display is closed flat against the shell with even edges and no visible gaps.
common_mistakes: Trapping a flex under the display
Forgetting a bracket screw
Closing the display before the connectors are seated

steps.title: Test the battery
steps.instruction: Power on the iPad and charge it. Check that Settings > Battery shows a healthy status and that it holds charge over the next hours.
steps.expected_visual_state: The iPad boots to the home screen and shows it is charging with a battery percentage.
common_mistakes: Judging the result too early
Not letting the battery fully charge the first time
